_why: Findings from the assert-faithfulness check that a person has read and judged to be intended. The check compares the assertions in a changed file against the same assertions in the base and reports every difference it cannot account for, so an edit to an assertion usually means one of two things: a mistake, which is the case the rule exists for, or an intended change, which the rule cannot tell apart on its own. This list is where the second case is recorded, so that the judgement is visible in a diff where a reader can question it, and so that it survives into continuous integration instead of living in one person's memory. Its shape is one key per rule id, then one key per repository-relative path, then a list of entries, because one file can raise two findings under the same rule and a person who has read both records both. Each entry holds the text the assertion checks, the reason the change is intended, and, when the finding reports one, the line. An entry silences one finding: it takes the one it names, which is the finding sitting on the line it recorded whenever the finding reports one, and a second finding the same entry could have silenced is left reported, so a finding nobody read stays a finding. Two entries that could both match the same finding leave the second one stale. The safe direction runs both ways. Removing an entry puts the finding back under the check, which is safe: the check then fails loudly on a finding it can no longer excuse, and the person who removed the entry sees that failure before anyone else does. Adding an entry is not safe in the same way. An entry written to silence a finding nobody read turns a working check into a list of things it no longer says, and that cost is invisible because the run goes green either way. An entry that matches no finding is reported as stale and fails the run, so this list cannot rot unnoticed and cannot grow into a blanket. A recorded line number must be the line the finding reports, and a mismatch fails the run rather than being ignored, because an entry that has slid onto a different assertion is an entry nobody wrote. Here is one rule and one path holding one entry, written as a person writes it rather than by a machine, so that nobody has to run the tool to find out what a record looks like: "_waivers": {"R1-changed": {"scripts/example.rs": [{"condition": "budget == 3", "reason": "the fake is given a budget of three now, and the assertion says so", "line": 42}]}}. The rule is the one the finding printed. The path is the file the finding's own line named, spelled exactly as it printed it. The condition is the claim the finding printed. The line is the line the finding reported, and it is left out only when the finding reported none, which is the case for a removed assertion. Copy the path out of your own finding line rather than from here: no tree holds scripts/example.rs, and a record naming a path that no run compares is named on every run and waives nothing. This file is the only sanctioned way to record an intended assertion change, and skipping the check from the command line is not one: a run that is not made is not an inspection, and nothing else in the tree records the judgement.
